Subject: MDR reportability assessment - coating adhesion

Priya, Bill, Rachel,

I have completed my regulatory review of the KinetiCoat adhesion failures observed at Northgate Health System and Presbyterian Denver.

1. MDR Reportability: Under 21 CFR 803.50, a device malfunction must be reported if the malfunction would be likely to cause or contribute to a death or serious injury if it were to recur. While the coating flaking occurred prior to implantation during unpacking, should an compromised cup be implanted without detection, loose titanium particulate and loss of fixation would reasonably necessitate surgical revision to prevent permanent impairment. Consequently, I have determined both events meet reportability criteria. Devon Mitchell and I intend to submit the initial 30-day MDRs to CDRH by Friday, April 15, well within the statutory deadline.

2. Field Action / Correction & Removal: Based on Bill's root-cause update from Cork tracing the parameter drift in the plasma-spray chamber across lots V-2200 through V-2299, the scope is substantial. Given the number of potentially affected units already distributed to the field, we must evaluate whether a voluntary Class II recall under 21 CFR 806 is formally required.

Rachel—please advise on timing and protocol for notifying outside counsel prior to our convening the recall committee.

Regards,

Dana

VP Regulatory Affairs
Veridian Orthopedics, Inc.

1. Summary of 2022 Objectives and Results

My principal objective for 2022 was to maintain regulatory compliance and timely agency communication while managing several high-priority product matters. I believe the Regulatory Affairs organization met this objective under unusually compressed timelines.

a. ApexHip field action. I provided regulatory oversight for the voluntary Class II recall initiated June 14, 2022, concerning KinetiCoat adhesion failures in ApexHip acetabular cup lots V-2200 through V-2299. This included review and approval of the recall strategy, customer notification materials, FDA submissions, distribution records, and effectiveness-check protocol. The affected population was 1,140 distributed units, of which 412 had been implanted as of the recall initiation.

b. FDA correspondence. I maintained primary executive oversight of correspondence with FDA CDRH and the Office of Compliance, including follow-up commitments arising from the 2021 inspection and Form 483 response. During 2022, the team ensured that required reports and recall-related updates were submitted within applicable timeframes. I also reviewed regulatory assessments relating to complaint trending and Medical Device Reporting obligations under 21 CFR Part 803, with particular attention to documentation supporting reportability determinations.

c. Legal preservation and cross-functional coordination. Following engagement of Whitfield & Barr and implementation of the February 1, 2022 litigation hold, I worked with Legal, Quality, R&D, Post-Market Surveillance, Commercial, and IT to ensure Regulatory Affairs materials were identified and preserved. This required practical coordination across Agile, TrackWise, shared drives, and individual custodian records. My role was limited to regulatory record identification and continued compliance obligations; Legal directed the hold process.

2. Leadership and Team Development

The Regulatory Affairs team continued to operate effectively despite increased volume, external scrutiny, and significant interdepartmental demands. I prioritized clear ownership of FDA commitments, escalation of deadline risks, and written documentation of decision-making. Devon Mitchell assumed increased responsibility for submission tracking and draft correspondence, which has improved continuity and reduced avoidable late-stage review issues.

3. Areas for Improvement

I would like to further formalize the interface between complaint handling, PMS, and Regulatory Affairs. Although the functions worked collaboratively, the volume and complexity of Apex-related matters demonstrated that escalation criteria can be clearer and more consistently documented. In 2023, I intend to implement a more regular cross-functional review cadence and written action log.

4. Compensation Consideration

I respectfully request that Rob consider a discretionary bonus component tied to successful closure of the ApexHip recall. The recall has required sustained senior-level oversight beyond the original annual objectives, including FDA communications, customer-facing regulatory review, and coordination of closure documentation. Any such consideration should be contingent on completion of effectiveness checks and FDA acceptance of recall closure materials.

Dana

URGENT: MEDICAL DEVICE RECALL NOTICE
ApexHip™ Acetabular Cup (Lots V-2200 through V-2299)
FDA Recall Number: Z-1418-2022

June 22, 2022

Attn: Materials Management & Surgical Services
Northgate Health System
(Affiliation: VantageOne GPO)
1200 Northgate Parkway
Minneapolis, MN 55407

Dear Director of Materials Management:

This letter is to notify Northgate Health System of a voluntary Class II medical device recall initiated by Veridian Orthopedics on June 14, 2022, regarding specific lots of the ApexHip Acetabular Cup.

1. Affected Product Details
- Product Name: ApexHip Acetabular Cup
- Model / Catalog Prefix: V-2
- Affected Lots: V-2200 through V-2299 inclusive
- Manufacturing Dates: November 2021 through February 2022
- Manufacturing Facility: Veridian Orthopedics, Cork, Ireland
- Distribution Scope: A total of 1,140 units across these lots were distributed nationally.

2. Reason for Recall
Veridian Orthopedics has identified an adhesion defect in the KinetiCoat porous titanium coating on the exterior surface of the cups in the referenced lots. In two reported instances during incoming inspection at customer facilities, localized flaking of the titanium coating was observed upon unwrapping the sterile packaging. Internal root-cause analysis determined that this defect resulted from transient plasma-spray parameter drift during coating application following scheduled vacuum chamber maintenance at our Cork manufacturing facility.

3. Required Customer Actions
Please immediately implement the following steps per standard hospital recall procedures:
1. Examine your inventory across all surgical suites, central sterile supply, and satellite storage locations to locate any ApexHip acetabular cups from lots V-2200 through V-2299.
2. Immediately quarantine and cease distribution or surgical use of all identified units.
3. Complete the enclosed Customer Recall Response & Reconciliation Form, indicating the number of unused units identified in your inventory, and email the completed form to Veridian Regulatory Affairs at regulatory@veridianortho.com within ten (10) business days of receipt.
4. Your Veridian Orthopedics sales representative will coordinate return shipping authorization and replacement product orders for all quarantined units.

If your facility has distributed any affected units to affiliated surgical centers within Northgate Health System, please ensure this notice is forwarded immediately.

We sincerely regret the inconvenience this action may cause your clinical staff and surgical operations. If you have questions regarding product return logistics or this regulatory notification, please contact Veridian Regulatory Affairs directly at (574) 555-0144.

Sincerely,

Dana Okonkwo
Vice President, Regulatory Affairs
Veridian Orthopedics, Inc.
dokonkwo@veridianortho.com

MEMORANDUM

TO: Priya Raman, Director of Quality & Complaint Handling; Carlos Mendes, Product Manager, ApexHip
FROM: Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip
DATE: January 10, 2022
SUBJECT: Engineering Status Review: ECO-2019-118 (Apex Acetabular Cup Rim Geometry & Clearance) — Closing the Loop

I am writing to formally revisit the open engineering posture surrounding ECO-2019-118. It has now been nearly three years since I submitted the initial Engineering Change Order proposal in February 2019, and our Design History File (DHF) index still does not accurately capture where we stand on this.

To recap the technical history: during the development phase leading up to Design Review 3 (DR-3) in November 2016, our wear simulator protocol was established strictly under ISO 14242-1 standard parameters, testing acetabular component placement at a nominal 45° inclination angle only. The Meridian Testing Labs reports confirmed acceptable volumetric wear under those ideal, nominal conditions, which supported our 510(k) clearance (K162447). However, as I flagged in my February 2019 re-analysis memo, testing the system under steeper acetabular cup inclinations—specifically 55°—produced severe edge-loading dynamics. The wear simulator data showed a 4× to 6× increase in gravimetric and volumetric metal wear rates compared to the 45° baseline, driven by localized contact stresses at the cup rim during microseparation cycles.

ECO-2019-118 proposed an immediate modification to the acetabular rim radius and polar clearance profile to mitigate edge-loading wear at non-ideal cup angles (which clinical data shows occur frequently in real-world patient anatomy).

In mid-2019, leadership decided to formally defer ECO-2019-118. The stated rationale at the time centered on commercial friction: tooling changeout costs, scrap write-downs, and especially the timeline required for full mechanical and simulator requalification, which would have disrupted peak production volumes.

Here is my primary concern today: as of January 2022, three full years after we identified the 4–6× wear multiplier under steep angles, no design change has been implemented. None. The product currently being shipped from Warsaw and Cork retains the exact rim geometry cleared in 2017.

Furthermore, I reviewed the ApexHip DHF index in Agile last week and noticed ECO-2019-118 is marked as "Closed / Superseded by Commercial Labeling Review." This is factually incorrect and creates an audit vulnerability. The engineering risk was never resolved or designed out; it was *deferred*. We should not be relying solely on post-market technique guides or surgeon education to manage a mechanical wear condition that we know occurs once the cup tilts past 50°.

I recommend two immediate corrective actions:
1. Re-open the DHF index entry for ECO-2019-118 and formally designate its status as "Deferred — Pending Clinical Registry / Post-Market Review," explicitly noting that the original ISO 14242 protocol tested only 45° inclination and did not evaluate edge-loading conditions.
2. Reconvene the cross-functional engineering review team (Quality, Product Management, R&D) to decide whether we are going to requalify the modified rim tooling or leave the deferred status on the permanent record.

We have known about the edge-loading wear multiplier since early 2019. Leaving the change order in administrative limbo without a clear engineering resolution is a significant unaddressed risk.

Regards,

Tom Halvorsen
Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip
Veridian Orthopedics, Inc.

MINUTES

Registry Signal Review
Tuesday, September 14, 2021 | 9:00 AM – 11:05 AM Eastern
Location: The Hub, Conference Room Reserve

Attendees: Dana Okonkwo, Priya Raman, Greg Novak, Dr. Leon Adeyemi, Rob Castellano, Carlos Mendes, Devon Mitchell (minutes)

1. NJR/AJRR Review (Novak)
Greg walked through the March 2021 NJR annual report showing ApexHip's 5-year revision rate at 7.1% against a 3.2% class average for metal-on-metal systems. He noted the confidence interval is wide given cohort size but the direction is consistent and stable across two reporting cycles. Late-2021 AJRR preliminary figures show the same directional signal in the US population, though Greg cautioned the US cohort's inclination-angle distribution is not well characterized and may differ from the UK data.

2. Wear-Test Findings Revisit (Raman presenting for Halvorsen; Adeyemi comment)
Priya summarized Tom Halvorsen's February 2019 re-analysis at 55-degree cup inclination, showing 4-6x wear versus the 45-degree-only protocol used at DR-3 in November 2016. Dr. Adeyemi raised significant clinical concern, stating the edge-loading wear data lines up mechanistically with elevated Co/Cr and ARMD findings, and specifically referenced the August 2018 Atlanta cluster (three patients, Dr. Feld's practice) as an early real-world signal that in his view was not adequately connected to the wear-test data at the time. He stated he did not think the company could treat these as unrelated observations any longer.

3. Options Discussion
Dana walked through three options: (a) continue selling with a labeling update including a Dear Doctor letter and revised IFU inclination guidance; (b) market withdrawal; (c) a design change to cup geometry/coating. Carlos noted a withdrawal would have significant commercial and messaging implications given Apex is ~20%+ of company revenue, and that a design change (per ECO-2019-118, previously deferred) would take 12-18 months minimum. Dr. Adeyemi reiterated that a labeling update alone may not address the underlying wear mechanism but agreed it is a reasonable interim step provided complaint trending is materially improved.

4. Decision
Rob Castellano approved continuing to sell ApexHip, contingent on: (1) a Dear Doctor letter to surgeons addressing inclination angle and monitoring recommendations, to be finalized in October; and (2) enhanced MDR/complaint trending cadence per Priya's procedure, with monthly rather than quarterly review going forward. Rob asked that this decision and its clinical basis be clearly documented.

Action Items:
- Devon Mitchell: draft Dear Doctor letter, target completion early October 2021; coordinate with Dana on any related FDA correspondence.
- Priya Raman: implement monthly complaint trending review, effective immediately; report back to Dana and Rob in 30 days.
- Greg Novak: continue monitoring NJR/AJRR data quarterly and flag any material shift.
- Carlos Mendes: assess sales/marketing messaging implications of labeling update, coordinate with Anika Shah.
- Dr. Adeyemi: available to review draft Dear Doctor letter language for clinical accuracy.

Minutes prepared by Devon Mitchell.

Cc: Carlos Mendes, Product Manager, ApexHip
Subject: Re-test results at 55 degree inclination - concerning wear rates

Priya, Carlos,

I'm writing this up formally because I don't think an email does it justice. As some of you know I've been unhappy with the DR-3 wear-test protocol for a while now — we only ran ISO 14242 at the standard 45 degree cup inclination, which is fine per the standard but doesn't reflect what I'm seeing in surgeon feedback about cup placement in the field. So I asked Meridian to re-run a set of samples at 55 degrees to see what happens.

The results are bad. Attached is Apex_wear_55deg_rev2.xlsx — columns are inclination angle, wear volume (mm3/million cycles), and head diameter. At 45 degrees we're seeing our expected baseline, roughly 0.8-1.2 mm3/Mc depending on head size (36-44mm range tested). At 55 degrees the same lots are producing 4-6x that volume, in the 4.5-6.8 mm3/Mc range. This is edge loading — the head is contacting the rim of the cup instead of the deep articulating surface, and at that inclination the wear mechanism basically changes character. It's not a small effect and it's not noise, I re-ran three sample sets and got the same pattern each time.

The uncomfortable question is how many of our implanted cups are sitting at 50+ degrees of inclination in actual patients. I don't have great visibility into that — that's more Priya's world with complaint data and maybe something Novak could pull from registry angle data if it's even captured — but anecdotally I know cup positioning varies a lot surgeon to surgeon, and nobody is checking inclination angle at 45 degrees with a protractor in the OR. If even a meaningful minority of our patients are outside the tested envelope, we have a real gap between what we validated and what's happening clinically.

I think we need to look seriously at the cup rim geometry. A few options I'd want on the table: increasing rim coverage/height to reduce edge contact at higher inclinations, revisiting the head-to-cup clearance, or possibly a chamfer redesign. None of these are trivial changes to a cleared device but I don't think we can just sit on this data.

I'd like to convene a design review — not a full DR, but something focused — to walk through this and talk about whether we open an ECO. I can have a full test report finished within two weeks but wanted you both to see the raw numbers now rather than wait.

Let me know your thinking. I'd rather over-communicate this than have it sit in my inbox.

Tom

Discussion Summary
Priya Raman reviewed the three complaints: TW-2018-0311, TW-2018-0322, and TW-2018-0340. All three originated from Dr. Marcus Feld’s Atlanta Joint Institute practice and involve patients revised following pain, elevated cobalt/chromium findings, and imaging or intraoperative observations requiring further review. Per procedure, the complaints will remain open pending complete medical records, retrieval information, and any additional laboratory results.

Tom Halvorsen reported preliminary observations from the returned femoral heads. Two of the three retrieved heads show wear patterns consistent with edge loading, including localized polishing and damage outside the expected primary bearing track. The third retrieval is incomplete and cannot yet be evaluated to the same extent. Tom cautioned that the observations are preliminary and that explant orientation, cup position, patient activity, and surgical factors have not been fully assessed. He recommended a formal wear analysis, including comparison with retained samples and available cup inclination information.

Greg Novak presented Q3 complaint-trending data. In the group of lots associated with the three Atlanta reports, the complaint rate is approximately 1.4%, compared with a 0.3% baseline rate across the remaining ApexHip population. Greg noted the numbers are small and should be interpreted cautiously; however, the difference warrants continued monitoring, particularly for metal-ion, pain, early revision, and ARMD-related coding. He will continue trend review through Q4 and circulate an updated summary.

Dana Okonkwo confirmed that two MDRs have been filed with FDA for events meeting reporting criteria. The third complaint remains under evaluation for reportability as additional clinical information is obtained. Dana noted that complaint documentation and follow-up must remain timely and complete under 21 CFR 803 and 820 requirements.

No field action or product communication was recommended at this time. The group agreed that the available information supports further investigation and enhanced monitoring.

Tom

Subject: NJR 2021 annual report - ApexHip 5-year revision rate

Priya, Dana, Tom,

The UK National Joint Registry (NJR) 2021 annual data tables were released this morning. I pulled our extract and ran the survival curves for the primary total hip cohort.

The headline number is problematic: the ApexHip 5-year cumulative revision rate is currently sitting at 7.1% (95% CI: 6.2% – 8.1%). For comparison, the contemporary class average across uncemented metal-on-poly and ceramic constructs in the registry is tracking at 3.2% at the 5-year mark. Even when adjusting for age stratification and diagnosis (predominantly osteoarthritis in the active 45–65 subset), Apex is more than double the benchmark.

Most concerning is the revision diagnosis breakdown. A significant portion of the early failures in the registry cohort cite aseptic loosening, adverse soft tissue reaction, or pain secondary to metallosis. This directly mirrors the trajectory we have been observing internally in TrackWise with the metal-ion complaint trend dating back to the Atlanta cluster in August 2018 (e.g., TW-2018-0882 et seq.) and the subsequent adverse reaction reports. The registry signal and our internal vigilance data are now pointing to the exact same failure mode.

Given the magnitude of the delta, we cannot treat this as standard PMS monitoring. I strongly recommend escalating this to a formal Registry Signal Review meeting with Leon and Carlos. Depending on how the clinical review lands, we may need to evaluate our continued marketing stance and labeling updates in short order.

Let me know your availability later this week to walk through the Kaplan-Meier plots.

Regards,

Greg Novak

Date: November 2, 2021
Prepared by: Carlos Mendes, Product Manager, ApexHip
Subject: Rep Training Deck: Fall 2021 Refresh

Deck file: Fall_2021_Reconstructive_Refresh_vFinal.pptx
Audience: U.S. Reconstructive Sales Organization
Delivery: Regional virtual sessions, November 8–19

Purpose of the refresh is to keep the field aligned on the portfolio story heading into year-end contracting, particularly where competitors are using isolated registry statistics or broad product-category concerns to create uncertainty. Please use the approved slides and speaker notes as written. Questions outside the materials should be routed to Product Marketing or Regulatory.

Slide 1 — Welcome / Fall Priorities
Open with the portfolio: KneeFlex momentum, continued ShoulderPro account expansion, and disciplined ApexHip customer support. Reminder that local market dynamics differ, but the core Veridian message should not.

Slide 2 — KneeFlex: Confidence Through Motion
KneeFlex remains our primary growth platform in knees. Position around reproducible instrumentation, workflow familiarity, and early surgeon experience. Avoid comparative survivorship statements unless the approved comparison slide is used in full. For accounts asking about the minor complaint trend discussed at summer meetings, state that Quality monitors all product feedback per procedure and that the product remains available.

Slide 3 — KneeFlex Objections
Common objection: “I have heard your tibial tray is difficult to revise.”
Suggested response: “KneeFlex was designed with revision workflow in mind, and we can arrange a technical discussion with one of our experienced users.” Do not speculate on individual cases or provide clinical advice.

Slide 4 — ShoulderPro Pricing and Value
For ShoulderPro, lead with system breadth and instrument efficiency. The approved price corridor remains in the regional pricing guide. Do not trade implants for capital commitments without Finance approval. Where a customer requests a bundled reconstruction proposal, involve the regional manager early.

Slide 5 — ApexHip: Current Positioning
ApexHip continues to offer the stability benefits associated with its large-diameter bearing option for appropriately selected patients. Keep the conversation clinical and surgeon-led. Do not use “lifetime” language, “zero wear,” or any unapproved durability claim. The current labeling is the governing source for indications, contraindications, warnings, and follow-up considerations.

Slide 6 — ApexHip: Questions on Metal Ions and the Label Update
This is the section to use if a surgeon asks about metal ions, revision reports, or the October Dear Doctor communication.

Recommended opening:
“I understand why you are asking. Veridian has updated the ApexHip labeling to provide additional guidance on patient selection and follow-up. We sent the Dear Doctor letter in October so surgeons would have the same information directly and in writing.”

If asked, “Are metal ions a new problem?”
Do not say “no issue,” “rare only,” or “nothing has changed.” Instead:
“Metal ion levels and metal-on-metal bearings are established clinical considerations. The updated labeling describes the factors physicians should consider, including patient selection, component positioning, and appropriate follow-up. I can make sure you have the letter and connect you with our clinical or medical team for questions specific to your practice.”

If a surgeon says, “Should I stop using Apex?”
Suggested response:
“That is a clinical decision for you and your patient. ApexHip remains available, and the labeling has been updated to support informed use. I can walk through the updated language, but I cannot advise you on an individual patient.”

Key point: do not characterize the October letter as a “warning,” “recall,” or “admission.” It is a physician communication accompanying an updated label. Do not minimize it either. Surgeons should not hear a different version from us than they received in the letter.

Slide 7 — Discussing the Updated Label Without Creating Unnecessary Alarm
Use a calm, direct transition:
“You may have seen the updated ApexHip label. The update gives more specificity around the patient population, surgical considerations, and follow-up that are important for this bearing.”

Then pause and let the surgeon respond. Do not fill the silence with unpublished data, personal opinions, or claims about what other surgeons are doing. If pressed on revision-rate figures or registry data, acknowledge the question and escalate to Medical Affairs/Post-Market Surveillance. Reps should not interpret registry tables in the field.

Bring printed copies of the Dear Doctor letter only where approved by your manager. The current electronic copy is in the sales portal under ApexHip > Clinical Resources > October 2021 Label Communication.

Slide 8 — Close / Escalation
For product complaints, obtain the available details and submit through the normal complaint process immediately. For clinical questions, use the Medical Information intake route. For commercial objections, involve your RSM and Product Marketing. Consistency matters more than having an instant answer.

Labeling Update Regarding Surgical Technique and Cup Positioning

Dear Dr. Anand:

Veridian Orthopedics, Inc. ("Veridian") is submitting this courtesy notification to inform the Agency of a voluntary update to the Instructions for Use (IFU) and surgical technique manual for the ApexHip Total Hip System, cleared under 510(k) K162447.

This labeling update incorporates refined clinical guidance emphasizing the critical importance of optimal acetabular cup positioning during implantation. Specifically, the updated labeling provides explicit instructions regarding target cup inclination angles (recommending placement within 40° to 45°) and anteversion parameters to mitigate potential edge-loading phenomena.

The rationale for this update stems from post-market surveillance monitoring, specifically data published in the March 2021 National Joint Registry (NJR) 18th Annual Report. The NJR report identified a cumulative 5-year revision rate of 7.1% for the ApexHip system, compared to a class benchmark of 3.2% for total hip arthroplasty systems within the same registry category. Subsequent internal technical evaluations and clinical reviews conducted by Veridian indicate that suboptimal cup inclination angles exceeding recommended parameters substantially increase contact stress and component wear.

Concurrently with this IFU update, Veridian is issuing an informational Dear Healthcare Provider ("Dear Doctor") communication in October 2021 to all active orthopedic surgeons utilizing the ApexHip system to reinforce these surgical technique parameters.

In accordance with 21 CFR 807.81(a)(3) and FDA guidance, "Deciding When to Submit a 510(k) for a Change to an Existing Device," Veridian has evaluated these modifications through our internal Design Controls and Change Assessment procedures. Because these updates add precautionary instructions and clarify existing surgical technique without altering the device's fundamental scientific technology, intended use, or indications, Veridian has determined that these changes do not significantly affect safety or effectiveness and do not require a new 510(k) submission.

Documentation supporting this internal evaluation has been placed in the Design History File (DHF). Veridian remains committed to proactive collaboration with CDRH. Please contact me directly at (574) 555-0182 or via email at dokonkwo@veridianortho.com should you require any additional information.

Priya and Dana,

I am writing this directly because I do not think this is appropriately handled through the usual field channel.

I have now performed six ApexHip revisions in my practice over approximately the past 18 months. These are not all identical presentations, but in most cases there were elevated cobalt levels, with chromium elevated as well, and visible metallosis at revision. Two had substantial soft-tissue reaction. I appreciate that six cases does not establish incidence, and I am reviewing the individual charts and imaging again, but it is enough that I need a clearer understanding of what Veridian is seeing more broadly.

Has the company identified a systemic issue with the device, whether related to positioning, edge loading, component design, or otherwise?

I recall being told informally in 2019 that there had been wear work at steeper cup angles that raised concerns beyond the standard test configuration. I was not provided the underlying data, and I did not press at the time. In light of what I am seeing now, I would like a direct answer as to what that work showed, what subsequent analyses or complaint trends have shown, and whether there is information that should affect my follow-up or counseling of Apex patients.

Given my prior consulting and royalty relationship with Veridian, it is especially important to me that I be fully informed. I cannot be in a position of learning material information after the fact from a patient, a registry report, or counsel.

Please let me know who can speak with me this week. I would prefer a substantive conversation, not generalized talking points.

Marcus

Dr. Marcus Feld
Atlanta Joint Institute

Subject: Notes - Rep Training Session 10/21

Marcus, Carlos—

Notes from today’s smaller Apex objection-handling session. Sarah Kim and Mike Ruiz attended, along with David Cole (Birmingham) and Erin Walsh (Knoxville). We worked through the updated FAQ and did four role-play scenarios.

Main scenario was the surgeon who has seen the NJR number and asks directly why Apex is at 7.1% at five years versus the 3.2% class average. Reps should not try to explain away the registry methodology, speculate about individual revisions, or characterize the figure as “not meaningful.” The approved approach is to acknowledge the question, reference the Dear Doctor letter and current labeling, and offer to connect the surgeon with Dr. Adeyemi for a clinical discussion.

Mike raised the fairly predictable follow-up: “Is this because the coating is coming off?” We also used a hypothetical packaging/incoming-inspection scenario involving a cup with visible coating flaking, since that is the kind of question a hospital buyer may put to a rep. Emphasis was that coating/adhesion questions and metal-ion or wear-performance questions are not the same issue and must never be conflated. Nobody should tell a customer that one proves or disproves the other.

Sarah was good on the redirect but initially added that the coating “wouldn’t affect anything once implanted.” We discussed not making that statement. If the question becomes clinical, product-performance-related, or patient-specific, stop and route it to Dr. Adeyemi/Medical Affairs. For product quality observations, send the details through the complaint process rather than trying to resolve it from the field.

Other reminders:
- Do not compare a surgeon’s own revision experience to the registry data.
- Do not promise a patient or surgeon that an implant will not require revision.
- Use the FAQ language; no improvised “off the record” answers.

Action item: Carlos to send the laminated pocket-card version of the FAQ to the Southeast and Nashville teams when available.

Jenna

FROM: Greg Novak (Director, Post-Market Surveillance)
DATE: March 22, 2021
SUBJECT: NJR 2021 Annual Report – ApexHip 5-Year Revision Rate Analysis

Executive Summary

The UK National Joint Registry (NJR) has released its 2021 Annual Report data tables, incorporating cumulative implant survival figures through December 31, 2020.

Our initial data extraction for the ApexHip Total Hip System reveals a statistically significant adverse survival divergence. The cumulative 5-year revision rate for ApexHip is reported at 7.1% (95% CI: 6.2%–8.1%), compared to a class benchmark of 3.2% (95% CI: 3.0%–3.4%) across contemporaneous metal-on-metal (MoM) and hybrid construct cohorts in the registry.

Cohort Breakdown and Timing of Divergence

The NJR dataset captures 4,128 primary ApexHip procedures performed across UK centers since CE mark entry in September 2017:

* Total Implants Tracked: 4,128 units (primarily 48mm–54mm acetabular cup sizes paired with matching Co/Cr femoral heads).
* Total Revisions Recorded: 184 cases.
* Revision Rate Trajectory:
    * Year 1: 1.2% (ApexHip) vs. 0.9% (Class average)
    * Year 2: 2.4% (ApexHip) vs. 1.7% (Class average)
    * Year 3: 4.6% (ApexHip) vs. 2.3% (Class average)
    * Year 5: 7.1% (ApexHip) vs. 3.2% (Class average)

The performance curve begins to diverge distinctly between months 24 and 36. Primary indications cited for revision within the NJR return entries include "pain of unknown origin," "aseptic loosening/cup migration," and "adverse soft tissue reaction" (accounting for roughly 48% of coded revision rationales past the 36-month mark).

Next Steps & Recommendations

1. AJRR Cross-Validation: We must correlate these findings against domestic performance immediately. American Joint Replacement Registry (AJRR) annual procedural datasets are slated for release later in 2021. I strongly recommend we prepare an identical query syntax to interrogate US revision trajectories as soon as that raw data cuts become available.
2. Clinical Assessment: I request Dr. Adeyemi’s formal clinical read regarding whether a 7.1% 5-year cumulative revision rate crosses our established Post-Market Clinical Follow-up (PMCF) internal action thresholds, particularly given the elevated proportion of soft-tissue and aseptic indications.
3. Formal Signal Review: Under our post-market surveillance SOPs, this variance warrants convening an interdepartmental Registry Signal Review meeting among Regulatory Affairs, Quality, Clinical, and Product Engineering to determine if labeling amendments, field communications, or formal CAPA escalation are required.

Please let me know your availability later this week to discuss these initial figures.

MEMORANDUM

Date: September 28, 2021
From: Dr. Leon Adeyemi, Chief Medical Officer
Subject: Clinical Assessment — ApexHip Revision Trend and Registry Signal
Distribution: Regulatory Affairs file / Design History File (ApexHip) / Post-Market Surveillance file

1. Purpose

This memo documents my clinical assessment of the ApexHip revision-rate signal identified in the March 2021 UK National Joint Registry (NJR) annual report, prepared in connection with the September 14, 2021 Registry Signal Review meeting, and is intended for inclusion in the regulatory record supporting the decision reached at that meeting.

2. Summary of Data

The NJR report identifies a 5-year revision rate for ApexHip of 7.1%, compared to a class average of approximately 3.2% for metal-on-metal and mixed-bearing large-head hip systems reporting to the registry. Preliminary review of AJRR data trends in the same direction, though with a smaller cohort and shorter follow-up. These are registry-level, retrospective signals; they are not derived from a controlled clinical study and are subject to the usual confounders (surgeon case mix, indication variation, reporting completeness).

3. Biological Plausibility

The published literature on metal-on-metal bearings, including work by Langton et al. and De Smet et al., establishes a well-characterized mechanism of edge loading at high cup inclination and anteversion angles, resulting in accelerated wear at the rim of the acetabular component and elevated cobalt/chromium ion release. This is consistent with Mr. Halvorsen's February 2019 internal re-analysis, which found 4- to 6-fold increases in wear rate at 55-degree inclination compared to the 45-degree condition used in our original ISO 14242 protocol. Taken together, the internal bench data and the external literature provide a biologically plausible mechanism for the registry-observed revision signal: patients whose cups are positioned outside the optimal inclination range are likely overrepresented among ApexHip revisions.

4. Clinical Assessment

I do not believe the currently available data establish that ApexHip carries an unacceptable risk profile for its labeled population when implanted within the intended positioning envelope. The revision rate elevation appears most plausibly attributable to a subset of cases with suboptimal cup positioning rather than a uniform device-level failure mode affecting all implanted systems. Absolute revision rates, while elevated relative to comparators, remain within a range seen historically for other metal-on-metal systems prior to their own market actions, and MDR volume to date has not shown a corresponding acceleration.

5. Recommendation

Based on the foregoing, I consider it clinically defensible to continue marketing ApexHip at this time, subject to the following:

a. Implementation of a labeling update emphasizing the importance of achieving cup inclination within the validated range and reinforcing appropriate patient selection;
b. Distribution of physician education materials, including a "Dear Doctor" letter, addressing cup positioning technique and encouraging use of intraoperative guidance where available;
c. Enhanced post-market surveillance, including closer tracking of MDR trends, AJRR data, and NJR updates on a quarterly basis rather than annual;
d. A structured re-review of this assessment within two quarters, or sooner if MDR volume, revision rate trending, or additional registry data show further deterioration.

I want to be clear that this recommendation is contingent on the surveillance measures above actually being implemented and reviewed on schedule. If the revision rate trend continues to climb, or if a subsequent registry cycle shows further separation from the class average, my assessment would need to be revisited and a market action would warrant serious reconsideration.

6. Conclusion

The available clinical and bench evidence supports continued marketing of ApexHip with the mitigations described above. This assessment should be read together with Mr. Novak's registry analysis and Ms. Raman's complaint trending summary, both prepared for the September 14 meeting.

Leon Adeyemi, MD
Chief Medical Officer

Purpose

This memo documents the 2021 annual performance review for Priya Raman, Director of Quality & Complaint Handling, reporting to Dana Okonkwo, VP Regulatory Affairs. Ratings and narrative below reflect input from Priya's self-assessment, manager feedback, and a calibration discussion held December 20, 2021.

Overall Rating: Meets Expectations / Exceeds in Select Categories

Strengths

Priya continues to run a tight complaint-handling operation. Her TrackWise intake and triage discipline remains a model for the department — complaint records are consistently well-documented, timeliness metrics for initial MDR determinations improved year over year, and her team's audit findings from the June 2021 FDA inspection (Warsaw) were limited and promptly addressed. Peer feedback from Regulatory and Quality consistently describes her as thorough, procedure-driven, and a steady hand during a difficult inspection year. She also mentored two complaint-handling specialists into stronger independent performance, which is reflected in reduced backlog numbers in Q4.

Area for Development

The primary development area identified this cycle relates to proactive escalation of complaint-trend signals to senior leadership, particularly where those trends intersect with external registry data. As context for this review, I want to note that in November 2021 the ethics hotline received an anonymous report raising concerns about the handling and internal escalation of complaint trends related to ApexHip. That matter has been referred through the appropriate channels for review and is being handled separately from this performance cycle; nothing in that report has been substantiated as attributable to Priya individually, and this review should not be read as a finding on that matter. It is noted here only because it forms part of the broader context considered in evaluating this development area.

Independent of the hotline matter, Dana's feedback — which Priya substantially agreed with in her self-assessment — was that trend summaries reaching leadership sometimes lag behind the underlying signal by several weeks, and that Priya's own written analyses tend to be conservative in flagging significance until a pattern is fully established. Given the volume and visibility of registry-related inquiries this year, both Priya and Dana agreed it would benefit the organization for Priya to escalate emerging signals earlier and with more explicit framing of risk, even before full trend confirmation, so leadership has visibility sooner.

Development Plan, FY2022

- Quarterly trend-escalation check-ins with Dana Okonkwo, in addition to standing complaint reviews.
- Priya to draft a revised escalation threshold/checklist for registry-adjacent complaint signals by end of Q1 2022.
- Continued participation in cross-functional Post-Market Surveillance reviews with Greg Novak's team to strengthen coordination between complaint trending and registry analysis.

Compensation/Advancement Note

No compensation action is recommended to change from standard merit cycle guidelines at this time; Priya remains in good standing and is viewed as a strong candidate for continued growth within Quality leadership.

VERIDIAN ORTHOPEDICS, INC.
PRODUCT MANAGEMENT MEMORANDUM

Date: January 15, 2020
From: Carlos Mendes, Product Manager, Hip Portfolio
Subject: ClassicHip Product Lifecycle Assessment

ClassicHip remains a clinically familiar and respected component of the Veridian hip portfolio, but its commercial and operational position no longer supports continued open-ended investment. Launched more than two decades ago, the system has served as our legacy metal-on-polyethylene offering through multiple generations of instrumentation and packaging updates. Its remaining demand is concentrated among a relatively small, aging group of surgeons who trained on the platform and continue to use it for selected cases.

Unit volume has declined each year since 2016, with the pace of decline accelerating following the 2017 launch of ApexHip. Apex has captured most new hip cases since launch, reflecting a change in market mix and surgeon preference rather than a near-term need to alter ClassicHip’s existing customer support commitments.

| Calendar Year | ClassicHip Systems Sold | Year-over-Year Change |
|---|---:|---:|
| 2016 | 4,200 | — |
| 2017 | 3,460 | (18%) |
| 2018 | 2,610 | (25%) |
| 2019 | 1,900 | (27%) |

The current 1,900-system run rate does not provide sufficient scale to offset the increasing fixed costs associated with maintaining a separate Warsaw manufacturing line, dedicated inventory positions, component tooling, supplier qualification activity, and ongoing commercial materials. Several lower-volume cup and stem configurations now require disproportionately frequent production scheduling and carry elevated obsolescence risk.

Commercial feedback indicates that a discontinuation, if managed carefully, should be workable. The remaining user base values predictability more than expansion of the platform. Distributors will need clear final-order dates, a defined service-parts period, and a straightforward migration conversation for accounts that currently use ClassicHip as their default metal-on-polyethylene option. We should avoid framing this as an abrupt exit or asking the field to force conversion on a fixed date without adequate inventory planning.

I recommend approval of a phased discontinuation over 24–36 months, subject to cross-functional confirmation of regulatory, quality, manufacturing, and customer-service requirements. The proposed approach is:

1. Freeze new product-development investment and new geographic expansion for ClassicHip in 2020.
2. Establish a controlled demand forecast by distributor and major account during the second quarter.
3. Set final order dates by product family, with advance written communication to distributors and affected hospital customers.
4. Maintain reasonable service inventory and instrument support through the transition period.
5. Develop field-facing migration materials that preserve customer choice and accurately describe available Veridian hip portfolio options.
6. Review remaining manufacturing-line economics quarterly with Warsaw Operations and Finance.

A preliminary planning assumption would be final distributor orders in the 2021–2022 period, followed by an orderly wind-down of routine manufacturing during the subsequent 12 months. Exact timing should depend on inventory commitments, regulatory record-retention obligations, and the ability of Warsaw to consolidate production without disrupting active product lines.

I recommend that Product Management convene a lifecycle working group by the end of January to validate the timeline and return with a final discontinuation recommendation for leadership approval.

Carlos Mendes

ENGINEERING DESIGN CHANGE MEMO

Date: 14 November 2023
Author: Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer
Subject: KneeFlex Revision Bearing Surface Design Update — ECO-2023-054
Distribution: Design History File, KneeFlex Revision

1. Purpose

This memo documents the proposed engineering change ECO-2023-054, addressing polyethylene bearing surface wear on the KneeFlex Revision system. The change is intended to reduce fine wear debris generation observed in post-market complaint data and to bring our wear-test protocol in line with a broader range of clinically relevant loading conditions.

2. Background

Complaint trending over the past 18 months (TW logs reviewed with Quality) shows a small but persistent cluster of revision cases citing increased polyethylene wear debris and localized osteolysis in KneeFlex Revision patients, particularly those with higher activity levels or off-nominal alignment. Root-cause review points to bearing surface geometry and edge-contact stress under non-ideal component positioning, not a material defect per se.

3. Proposed Design Change

The proposed change modifies the tibial insert bearing geometry to increase conformity at the articulating margin, reducing peak contact stress under off-axis loading. A revised FMEA has been drafted (KneeFlexRev_FMEA_rev4.xlsx, attached under separate cover) identifying "edge loading under high flexion/rotation" as a new failure mode with increased RPN relative to the prior FMEA baseline.

4. Wear Test Protocol Update

Historically our wear-test protocols for hip and knee lines have relied on a single inclination/loading condition per ISO guidance minimums. For this ECO, I'm proposing we test the new bearing geometry at both 45 and 60 degrees of effective loading angle to better capture off-nominal implantation scenarios, rather than relying on a single "nominal" condition and assuming it bounds the worst case. Meridian Testing Labs has been asked for a quote on a dual-angle protocol; results should be available by Q1 2024.

Frankly, this is something we should have done years ago across other product lines — testing only at a single nominal angle gives you a clean number but it doesn't tell you what happens when a surgeon's inclination or version is a few degrees off nominal, which is exactly where we tend to see field complaints cluster. I raised something similar internally a while back and it didn't get traction at the time; I'd rather not repeat that here.

For reference, the hip program's original wear-test protocol adopted back in 2016 was scoped to a single 45-degree inclination condition only, consistent with the ISO 14242 minimum at the time. That was a narrower testing envelope than what I'm proposing here for KneeFlex Revision, though I recognize the hip program has its own separate history and I'm not trying to reopen that here — just flagging it as context for why I think the dual-angle approach is the right call going forward for any bearing surface design work.

5. Next Steps

- Finalize updated FMEA with Quality sign-off (target: end of November)
- Submit wear-test protocol to Meridian Labs for quoting
- Schedule design review DR-KFR-7 for early December to walk through proposed geometry change and updated risk file
- Coordinate with Regulatory (Mitchell) on whether this change triggers a new 510(k) or can proceed under a letter-to-file

Please route comments to me directly before DR-KFR-7. I'd like FMEA sign-off in hand before that meeting.

Tom Halvorsen
Sr. Design Engineer, KneeFlex Revision

meta.gray_rationale: The memo obliquely references the older hip wear-test protocol scope by analogy without naming ApexHip or giving substantive facts, so a reviewer could reasonably find it too indirect to be responsive to the design-history RFP.

From: it-help@veridianortho.com
To: all-hub-employees@veridianortho.com
Date: Mon, 02 Aug 2021 09:06
Subject: Phishing Alert: Fake DocuSign Emails

Veridian IT Security has received reports of a phishing campaign impersonating DocuSign.

The messages typically ask the recipient to review and sign a “contract renewal” document. They may include DocuSign branding and a link labeled “Review Document” or “Complete with DocuSign.”

Please do not click links or open attachments unless you were expecting the document.

Before responding to any DocuSign email:

- Check the sender’s full email address, not just the display name.
- Hover over links to verify the destination before clicking.
- Be cautious of unexpected signature requests, especially those creating urgency.
- Do not enter Veridian credentials on unfamiliar pages.

If you receive a suspicious message, forward it as an attachment to phishing@veridianortho.com and then delete it. If you clicked a link or entered your password, contact the Service Desk immediately.

IT Service Desk
Veridian Orthopedics

Subject: Cork line capacity if ClassicHip winds down

Carlos,

Following up on the planning call, if ClassicHip is wound down on the current timetable, Cork would free roughly 22–26 machining hours per week on Line 2, plus inspection and pack-out capacity. That assumes we run down the remaining legacy cup and liner schedule rather than stopping cold.

The practical choices for the space are:

1. Additional Apex cup machining / KinetiCoat cup volume, if demand continues as forecast. We could support approximately 300–350 additional cups per month without a major capital request, though scheduling would need to be tightened around the existing Apex runs.

2. KneeFlex components. The knee team has asked informally whether we can take some of the smaller machined components. That is feasible, but it would require fixtures and a modest validation package, so it is not as immediate as simply adding Apex volume.

3. Maintain some capacity as a buffer. I would recommend we do not allocate every available hour on paper. The line is already carrying a fair amount of changeover activity.

For reference, the facility is currently averaging about 78% scheduled utilization across machining, with finishing nearer 70%. Pack-out has more room than either area.

Happy to put together a more detailed capacity view for your portfolio planning deck. The main decision point is whether ClassicHip’s final production date is firm enough to treat those hours as available.

Regards,

Bill Kowalski

FORM QMS-402: PRODUCT COMPLAINT INVESTIGATION & CLOSURE SUMMARY

PART I: COMPLAINT DETAILS
* Complaint Tracking ID: TW-2023-0812
* Date Opened: 2023-08-22
* Date Closed: 2023-10-16
* Investigator: Priya Raman, Director, Quality & Complaint Handling
* Product Name: ClassicHip System (Legacy Femoral Stem & Polyethylene Acetabular Liner)
* Part Numbers / Lot Numbers: Stem: CH-7012 (Lot S-1104); Liner: CH-4402 (Lot L-8821)
* Reporter: Dr. H. Vance, Cleveland Orthopedic Center, OH
* Initial Event Description: Revision of left hip arthroplasty after 11 years in situ. Operating surgeon reported mechanical loosening of the femoral component and mild acetabular wear.

PART II: INVESTIGATION FINDINGS
1. Device History Record (DHR) Review: Completed for stem lot S-1104 and liner lot L-8821. All manufacturing parameters met release specifications at time of release (2012). No non-conformances identified.
2. Explant Analysis: Femoral stem and ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene (UHMWPE) liner were returned to the Hub on 2023-09-15. Visual inspection and dimensional metrology show expected volumetric polyethylene wear along the superior weight-bearing quadrant consistent with 11+ years of implantation. No evidence of gross mechanical defect or unexpected material degradation.
3. Medical Device Reporting (MDR) Determination: Evaluated per 21 CFR 803. Event determined to be revision due to late-stage aseptic loosening and standard poly wear. No reportable malfunction or unexpected adverse event identified; MDR not required.
4. Trending & Phase-Out Note: ClassicHip is currently under scheduled product discontinuation with minimal active inventory remaining. Complaint rates for the legacy metal-on-polyethylene system remain well below established alert limits (current rolling 12-month rate: 0.18%). Findings are entirely consistent with known long-term UHMWPE wear characteristics.

PART III: CORRECTIVE ACTION & CLOSURE
* CAPA Required: No.
* Closure Rationale: Investigation complete. Cause confirmed as normal wear pattern typical of legacy polyethylene bearings after prolonged service life. No systemic quality issue indicated.

Approved By: Priya Raman

VERIDIAN ORTHOPEDICS, INC.
ENGINEERING TECHNICAL REPORT

REPORT NUMBER: ETR-2021-0084
TITLE: Design Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (DFMEA) Annual Update – KneeFlex Revision System
AUTHOR: Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer, Knee & Hip R&D
DATE: February 15, 2021
STATUS: Released / Approved
DOCUMENT CONTROL: Agile PLM / DHF-KF-0042

1. Purpose & Scope

This report documents the periodic review and formal update of the Design Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (DFMEA-KF-REV, Rev 04) for the KneeFlex Revision Total Knee System. The primary focus of this update involves:
1. Re-evaluating risk priority numbers (RPNs) associated with backside polyethylene wear and tibial baseplate locking mechanism tolerances.
2. Incorporating post-market surveillance (PMS) feedback regarding intraoperative instrument mating tolerances between the revision femoral cutting blocks and the standard KneeFlex primary resection guides.
3. Updating stem extension taper lock integrity models under non-axial revision loading profiles.

This review encompasses the KneeFlex Revision femoral components (Sizes 2–6), modular constrained condylar inserts (CCK), augmented tibial baseplates, and titanium modular stem extensions (straight and offset).

2. Failure Mode Analysis & Updates

2.1 Tibial Tray / Polyethylene Backside Wear (Line Items 4.12 – 4.16)
Post-market observation from 2020 explant evaluations identified micro-motion at the junction of the CCK revision insert and the augmented tibial baseplate in cases with severe ligamentous laxity.

* Failure Mode: Sub-millimeter toggle of CCK insert locking tab under high varus/valgus constraint moments.
* Potential Effect: Generation of sub-micron polyethylene debris leading to localized osteolysis along the proximal tibial plateau.
* Initial Risk Score: Severity (S) = 7, Occurrence (O) = 3, Detection (D) = 3 → RPN = 63.
* Mitigation / Action Taken: Tightened machining tolerances on the posterior peripheral locking rim (Drawing DWG-KF-3302) from ±0.05 mm to ±0.02 mm. FEA analysis confirms that reducing permissible interface gap eliminates rotational toggle under cyclic 1.5 kN joint loads.
* Revised Risk Score: Severity (S) = 7, Occurrence (O) = 2, Detection (D) = 2 → RPN = 28. Residual risk is deemed acceptable per SOP-RD-202.

2.2 Stem Extension Modular Taper Junction Wear & Fretting (Line Items 5.03 – 5.07)
Modular stems (straight 100mm/150mm and 2mm/4mm offset adapters) utilize a 12/14 Morse-style taper secured with an internal titanium locking screw.

* Failure Mode: Insufficient torque application to locking screw intraoperatively, leading to micro-motion at the taper junction under bending moments exceeding 85 Nm.
* Potential Effect: Fretting corrosion at the Ti-6Al-4V to Ti-6Al-4V interface; eventual stem loosening or pain.
* Initial Risk Score: S = 6, O = 3, D = 4 → RPN = 72.
* Mitigation / Action Taken: Verification testing (Report TR-20-441) confirmed that the taper geometry remains mechanically stable up to 110 Nm when torqued to 5.0 Nm. The surgical technique guide (STG-KF-02) has been revised to require the reusable preset 5.0 Nm torque wrench (Part # KT-9941) rather than the standard cross-pin driver. Torque wrench calibration cycle added to hospital instrument processing labeling.
* Revised Risk Score: S = 6, O = 2, D = 2 → RPN = 24. Residual risk acceptable.

2.3 Revision Instrument Compatibility & Interface Interference (Line Items 8.01 – 8.09)
Field reports indicated occasional binding when passing the 14mm revision intramedullary reamer through the primary KneeFlex distal femoral resection guide block.

* Failure Mode: Dimensional interference between reamer shaft bushing and resection guide slot.
* Potential Effect: Intraoperative delay, metal shavings generated from cutting guide contact if misaligned.
* Initial Risk Score: S = 4, O = 4, D = 2 → RPN = 32.
* Mitigation / Action Taken: Engineering Change Order ECO-2020-089 implemented a 0.25 mm chamfer on the interior bushing entrance and increased the guide bore clearance. Mating verification protocols confirmed smooth passage through 100% of tolerance-stack combinations.
* Revised Risk Score: S = 4, O = 1, D = 2 → RPN = 8.

3. Summary Risk Table

| Item | Component | Failure Mode | Initial RPN | Action / Control | New RPN |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4.14 | CCK Tibial Insert | Insert-to-tray micromotion | 63 (7×3×3) | Tightened rim machining tolerances (DWG-KF-3302) | 28 (7×2×2) |
| 5.05 | Modular Stem | Taper fretting under bending | 72 (6×3×4) | Mandate calibrated 5.0 Nm torque driver in STG | 24 (6×2×2) |
| 8.04 | IM Reamer / Guide | Bushing interference / binding | 32 (4×4×2) | Chamfer bore and expand clearance (ECO-2020-089) | 8 (4×1×2) |

4. Conclusion & Recommendations

All updated failure modes within the KneeFlex Revision product line fall below the company threshold RPN of 40 following corrective design and labeling controls. No critical safety risks remain unmitigated. The revised DFMEA matrix has been uploaded to Agile under DHF-KF-0042 and is submitted for quality engineering routing.

Approved by:
*Tom Halvorsen*
Sr. Design Engineer, Knee R&D
Veridian Orthopedics, Warsaw, IN

RE: Medical Device Report (Initial 30-Day Narrative)
Device: ApexHip™ Acetabular Cup System
510(k) Number: K162447
Manufacturer: Veridian Orthopedics, Inc. (FEI: 1834921)
Internal TrackWise Records: TW-2022-0388; TW-2022-0402

Dear Regulatory Reviewer:

Veridian Orthopedics, Inc. is submitting this initial narrative report pursuant to 21 CFR Part 803 concerning two related complaint events received regarding the ApexHip™ Acetabular Component with KinetiCoat™ porous titanium coating.

1. Event Description:
On April 14, 2022, Veridian received notification from Northgate Health System regarding Lot V-2214 (TW-2022-0388). During incoming hospital inspection and visual check prior to package unwrapping in central sterile processing, the clinical staff observed localized flaking and particulate shedding of the KinetiCoat porous coating along the rim and exterior shell.

On April 22, 2022, a second incident was reported by Denver Health Medical Center involving Lot V-2231 (TW-2022-0402). Similarly, incoming hospital inspection identified visible delamination of the porous plasma-spray coating within the sterile inner blister pack upon receipt.

2. Patient Impact:
In both reported instances, the condition was identified prior to surgery during routine receiving inspection. The devices were immediately sequestered by the respective facilities and returned to Veridian. Neither unit was implanted, and no patient contact or adverse clinical event occurred.

3. Investigation Status:
Both units were manufactured at Veridian Orthopedics' Cork, Ireland facility. Veridian's Quality Engineering and Manufacturing teams have initiated an internal investigation to determine root cause, focusing on manufacturing batch records, environmental controls, and plasma-spray deposition chamber parameters during the relevant production periods (November 2021 through February 2022).

Veridian will submit a supplemental report upon completion of the root cause investigation, including any corrective actions or field action determinations regarding affected product lots.

Sincerely,

Devon Mitchell
Senior Regulatory Specialist
Veridian Orthopedics, Inc.

From: Devon Mitchell <dmitchell@veridianortho.com>
To: prashant.anand@fda.hhs.gov
Cc: Dana Okonkwo <dokonkwo@veridianortho.com>
Date: Mon, 3 Jun 2019 15:12:44 -0400
Subject: RE: Additional Information Request - MDR Trending Analysis

Dear Dr. Anand,

On behalf of Veridian Orthopedics, Inc., please find below our formal response to the Agency's May 8, 2019 inquiry regarding the ApexHip Total Hip System (510(k) K162447 / Post-Market Review). Attached to this submission is our detailed MDR and TrackWise complaint trending summary (Attachment 1: ApexHip_MDR_Trending_Analysis_2019.pdf).

Summary of Post-Market Surveillance Trending and Engineering Assessment:

1. Complaint Trending: A comprehensive review of our post-market surveillance database (TrackWise) confirms that exactly 14 metal-ion related complaints (associated with elevated cobalt/chromium levels, suspected ARMD, or early revision) have been logged since commercial launch in April 2017 through April 30, 2019. This represents an overall reporting rate of less than 0.2% across all commercially distributed ApexHip acetabular cups and femoral heads during this period, which remains well below internal statistical alert thresholds established under SOP-QC-408.

2. Clinical and Engineering Evaluation: In coordination with Medical Affairs and R&D Engineering, Veridian has reviewed available clinical histories and explant reports. A substantial proportion of reported events exhibit localized surgical variables, including high cup abduction angles. While the company's PMS program continues to closely monitor this trend, the cumulative data indicate that the device performs in accordance with its cleared safety profile. Consequently, no design change or corrective action has been deemed necessary at this time based on available clinical data.

Veridian remains fully committed to regulatory compliance under 21 CFR Part 803 and 21 CFR 820.198 and will continue providing routine updates as required.

Sincerely,

Dana Okonkwo
Vice President, Regulatory Affairs
Veridian Orthopedics, Inc.
dokonkwo@veridianortho.com

(Transmitted by Devon Mitchell, Sr. Regulatory Specialist, dmitchell@veridianortho.com)

The Division of Orthopedic Devices is currently conducting routine post-market surveillance oversight regarding the ApexHip Total Hip System (K162447).

In our review of Medical Device Reports (MDRs) submitted by Veridian Orthopedics under 21 CFR Part 803 over the past 18 months, CDRH has noted an increased frequency of adverse event reports citing elevated cobalt and chromium ion levels, local tissue reactions, and early revision procedures. Specifically, we have reviewed the cluster of reports originating from the Atlanta, Georgia area initially submitted between August and October 2018.

From: Tom Halvorsen <thalvorsen@veridianortho.com>
To: Priya Raman <praman@veridianortho.com>; Carlos Mendes <cmendes@veridianortho.com>
Date: Mon, 11 Feb 2019 07:18
Subject: 55-degree wear retest results - concerning

Priya, Carlos—

I re-ran the ISO 14242 wear simulation at 55° cup inclination rather than the 45° orientation used in the DR-3 protocol. Results are attached: Apex_wear_55deg_rev2.xlsx.

Short version: this is not a marginal difference.

At 55°, the wear rate is 4–6x higher than the 45° baseline depending on head/cup combination. The damage is concentrated at the cup rim, with visible edge-loading/scoring rather than the more uniform pattern we saw under the original setup. Co/Cr debris generation tracks with that increase.

I know 55° is not the nominal surgical target, but it is not an exotic placement angle either. We have always known inclination varies in the field. Testing only at 45° gave us a clean result, but it does not appear to represent this condition.

Priya: I think we need to look at the Atlanta metal-ion cluster in TrackWise against cup position if we have radiographs or surgeon notes. This result could explain at least part of what is being reported there. I am not saying every elevated-ion complaint is this mechanism, but the correlation is concerning enough that we should not treat it as routine complaint noise.

Carlos: please do not turn this into a messaging exercise yet. First we need a design review. I want to discuss whether the cup geometry/rim needs to change, and whether there are interim limitations we should be considering.

Can we convene DR-4 this week? This is urgent, not a normal protocol follow-up.

Tom

Attachment: Apex_wear_55deg_rev2.xlsx

Subject: Recall Notification to FDA - Draft for Review

Devon, Bill, Priya:

Attached is the current draft of the voluntary recall notification to FDA for ApexHip acetabular cup lots V-2200 through V-2299. Please review against your respective records this evening. We intend to file tomorrow, June 14.

The draft identifies the affected product as ApexHip Co/Cr acetabular cups manufactured in Cork between November 2021 and February 2022, with KinetiCoat porous coating adhesion failures identified following incoming inspection reports from Northgate Health System and a Denver hospital. In both instances, coating flaking was observed upon unwrapping the device.

The distribution section presently states:

1. Total units distributed: 1,140.
2. Total units implanted: 412.
3. Remaining units are either in customer inventory, distributor inventory, returned, or in Veridian-controlled stock pending reconciliation.

The preliminary root-cause statement is that the adhesion issue has been traced to plasma-spray parameter drift following a chamber maintenance event at the Cork facility. We should be precise here: the investigation remains open, but the available batch-record review and chamber data support that conclusion. The notification does not characterize this as a field performance or metal-ion issue.

Bill, please confirm the final distributed, implanted, and on-hand/returned unit counts no later than 09:00 Eastern tomorrow. If there is any discrepancy between the lot trace and the figures above, send the supporting reconciliation rather than simply revising the total.

Priya, please confirm that the complaint descriptions and dates in the attached draft align with the TrackWise records and that no additional unreported coating-related complaints have been identified.

Devon, once Bill and Priya have confirmed, please finalize the Form FDA 3419 fields and prepare the submission package, including the proposed customer notification and consignee list. Ensure the classification rationale is consistent with the health hazard evaluation.

Please do not distribute the draft outside this group pending final review.

Dana

From: Greg Novak
To: Dana Okonkwo; Priya Raman
Date: Thu, 16 Jun 2022 09:47
Subject: Registry data post-recall - any change in ApexHip revision trend?

Dana, Priya,

Following up two days out from the recall announcement. Wanted to flag something before it gets asked at a higher level.

The V-2200–V-2299 recall is a coating adhesion issue traced to plasma-spray drift at Cork — mechanically it's unrelated to the revision-rate signal we've been tracking out of NJR (7.1% at 5 years vs. 3.2% class average) and the AJRR data. That signal is driven by edge-loading wear and elevated Co/Cr, not coating flaking at inspection. Different failure mode, different population — the recalled lots weren't even implanted long enough to be in the 5-year registry cohort.

That said, I'd bet money plaintiffs' counsel will try to blur the two, and honestly some surgeons will too once they hear "recall" and "ApexHip" in the same sentence. Dr. Whitaker in Denver already conflates every Apex complaint into one bucket.

I think it'd be smart to get ahead of this with a short internal FAQ that clearly separates the coating issue from the metal-ion/revision-rate issue, in plain language, in case the board or comms needs to respond to press or surgeon questions. I can draft a first pass on the registry side if Priya can cover the complaint-handling angle and Dana can sanity-check the regulatory framing.

Let me know if this makes sense to prioritize this week.

Greg

From: Kessler Reid <news@kesslerreid.com>
To: Anika Shah <ashah@veridianortho.com>; Carlos Mendes <cmendes@veridianortho.com>
Date: Thu, 14 Jan 2021 09:06
Subject: Kessler Reid Newsletter - Design Trends in Medical Marketing 2021

Happy New Year from Kessler Reid.

As healthcare organizations look ahead to 2021, we are seeing a continued move toward cleaner, calmer visual systems across patient and professional collateral. The past year has made clarity and confidence more important than ever; audiences want information that is easy to scan without feeling cold or overly clinical.

A few design trends our studio is watching:

• Warm minimalism. Neutral backgrounds paired with one confident accent color continue to replace dense, multi-color layouts.

• Human-centered photography. Authentic settings and natural expressions are outperforming heavily staged stock imagery, particularly in patient-facing materials.

• Typography with personality. Modern sans serif families remain the workhorse, but brands are introducing more distinctive type treatments for headlines. Larger type and generous spacing also improve readability across print and digital formats.

• Accessible color palettes. Deep blues, soft greens, muted terracottas, and high-contrast neutrals are appearing frequently. Accessibility review should remain part of every creative process, not an end-stage check.

• Modular content. Flexible page components allow a brochure, landing page, email, and social asset to feel connected while serving different reading behaviors.

We expect the strongest healthcare work this year will balance clinical credibility with a more approachable, optimistic visual tone.

Best,
Kessler Reid Creative Team

Attaching the draft root cause summary for CAPA-2022-0093 (KinetiCoat adhesion, cup lots V-2200 through V-2299). File is CAPA-2022-0093_RootCause_draft1.docx.

Short version: we traced it back to the chamber maintenance we did in early November after the plasma torch nozzle swap. Line techs recalibrated afterward but the post-maintenance verification run wasn't tight enough to catch a drift in the spray parameters - specifically powder feed rate and standoff distance crept outside the validated window for about a 12-week window before it got flagged in incoming inspection at the two hospitals. Batch records confirm the drift lines up with lots in that range, nothing before or after.

Proposed corrective actions:
1. Revised preventive maintenance checklist for the plasma spray chamber, adding explicit parameter checks post-maintenance, not just equipment function checks.
2. Mandatory calibration verification run with witness coupons before the line restarts production after any chamber maintenance event, sign-off required by both line lead and quality.
3. Tightened SPC alarm limits on feed rate and standoff distance so we catch drift earlier next time.

Want to flag clearly - this is a coating/manufacturing issue on the Cork line, root cause is process drift after maintenance. It's not related to the wear/metal-ion tracking Priya's team has going separately on the complaint side. Different animal entirely, just want to make sure that distinction stays clear in the CAPA file.

Let me know if you want changes before I route this for QA sign-off.

URGENT: IMPORTANT MEDICAL DEVICE INFORMATION
ApexHip Total Hip System (510(k) K162447)

Dear Orthopedic Surgeon:

The purpose of this letter is to provide updated clinical management recommendations regarding the Veridian Orthopedics ApexHip Total Hip System (cleared via 510(k) K162447 in March 2017). Veridian Orthopedics is committed to patient safety and continuous evaluation of post-market clinical performance.

Recent analyses of international and domestic joint replacement registries, including the National Joint Registry (NJR) of the United Kingdom and late 2021 observational subsets from the American Joint Replacement Registry (AJRR), have identified an elevated cumulative revision rate for the ApexHip system compared to historical polyethylene bearing benchmarks. Specifically, data indicate a 5-year cumulative revision rate trending higher than aggregate registry class averages, with an increased risk profile observed in implant cohorts utilizing larger femoral head diameters (44 mm to 50 mm) and in constructs where the acetabular cup component was positioned at higher inclination angles (exceeding 45 degrees).

In light of these post-market registry trends, Veridian Orthopedics recommends the following enhanced clinical monitoring protocols:

1. Routine Clinical Follow-Up: Schedule regular follow-up examinations for all implanted ApexHip patients at minimum annual intervals, regardless of current symptomatic presentation.
2. Cross-Sectional Imaging and Ion Testing: For patients presenting with persistent pain, unexplained groin discomfort, swelling, or mechanical clicking, perform cross-sectional imaging (such as MARS-MRI or high-resolution ultrasound) to evaluate for adverse local tissue reactions (ALTR/ARMD) and obtain serum cobalt and chromium ion concentration panels.
3. Component Evaluation: When assessing imaging, verify acetabular orientation and cup abduction angles to detect potential edge-loading phenomena.

Surgeons should continue to report any adverse events, unexpected revisions, or suspected tissue necrosis directly to Veridian Quality & Complaint Handling at complaints@veridianortho.com or via our medical safety hotline at 1-800-555-0194, which routes directly into our TrackWise complaint intake and regulatory surveillance system.

Sincerely,

Dana Okonkwo
Vice President, Regulatory Affairs
Veridian Orthopedics, Inc.

MEMORANDUM

TO: Commercial Operations, Regional Sales Directors, Regulatory Affairs
FROM: Carlos Mendes, Product Manager
DATE: September 11, 2023
SUBJECT: Commercial Notification Draft: ClassicHip System End-of-Life & Hospital Transition Guidance

Purpose & Executive Summary

As part of our ongoing portfolio rationalization strategy and the continued transition of our product lines to modern implant platforms, Veridian Orthopedics will formally sunset the ClassicHip Total Hip System. Effective January 31, 2024, the ClassicHip system—including all legacy femoral stems, modular heads, and standard metal-on-polyethylene acetabular cup components—will reach its formal End-of-Life (EOL) status.

Below is the draft of the customer-facing notice scheduled for release to hospital purchasing committees, materials management directors, and clinical department chairs on October 2, 2023. Please review the operational timing and messaging pillars before final layout by Kessler Reid.

Draft Customer Notice: Notice of Product Obsolescence

Date: October 2, 2023
To: Director of Materials Management / Chief of Orthopedic Surgery
Subject: Notice of Product Discontinuation: Veridian ClassicHip Total Hip System

Dear Valued Customer,

Since its commercial introduction in 2004, the Veridian ClassicHip Total Hip System has served as a reliable workhorse implant within primary hip arthroplasty, demonstrating a reliable clinical heritage anchored in traditional metal-on-polyethylene articulation. In addition to providing years of dependable service across thousands of procedures, the ClassicHip platform provided the fundamental predicate design history and technological baseline upon which subsequent generations of Veridian reconstructive systems were established.

However, advancements in implant metallurgy, advanced bearing surfaces, and modern fixation geometries have steadily shifted clinical preference toward newer reconstructive solutions. Consequently, Veridian Orthopedics will officially discontinue manufacturing and distribution of the ClassicHip system in accordance with the schedule below:

* Final Purchase Orders Accepted: December 15, 2023 (subject to remaining inventory availability)
* Official Commercial Discontinuation Date: January 31, 2024
* Instrument Tray Retrieval & Consignment Reconciliation: February 1, 2024 – March 31, 2024

Clinical Transition Support
Veridian remains dedicated to ensuring an uninterrupted supply of premium reconstructive options for your operating rooms. Your local sales representatives are actively coordinating with surgical teams to assist in transitioning accounts toward our broader reconstructive portfolio, ensuring appropriate instrument tray conversions, sterile supply alignment, and staff in-service training prior to the January 31 cut-off.

For facilities requiring continued access to legacy ClassicHip poly liners or modular head sizes for pending scheduled cases, please contact Customer Care to coordinate reserved lot allocations.

Internal Next Steps & Commercial Timeline

1. Inventory Reconciliation: Field sales leadership should review existing hospital consignment banks by October 13, 2023.
2. Contracting/GPO Adjustments: Commercial operations will issue formal deletion notices to GPO rosters (including VantageOne) effective Q1 2024.
3. Collateral Deprecation: All ClassicHip surgical techniques, brochures, and digital references will be archived from the portal on January 31, 2024.
